notes:
I've written notes on 22 of the 28 verses. There's nothing for vv. 1, 3, 10, 20, 23 or 24, because the pages I could open didn't discuss them.

The search tool cut me off before I could get to several sources. I didn't open Wesley's notes, any Lutheran or Pentecostal site besides Enduring Word, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, or any Orthodox site, and I found no material from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. Enduring Word's page also stopped partway through, so it only covers vv. 1–22.

The splits I did find on vv. 14, 16–17, 25–26 and 27 mostly run between individual teachers, not along denominational lines.

---

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:** The tabernacle was a two-room tent. The larger first room was the Holy Place, and the smaller inner room beyond the second veil was the Holiest of All. Guzik says the twelve loaves on the table stood for God's fellowship with Israel's twelve tribes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**v. 4**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the three objects inside the ark each reminded Israel of something. The manna recalled God's provision and the people's ingratitude. Aaron's rod recalled their rebellion. The tablets recalled their failure to keep the law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
- **The puzzle (incense altar vs. censer):** Exodus puts the incense altar in the outer room, so why is it listed with the inner room?
  - Ellicott says the "censer" reading spread mainly through the Vulgate, and most eminent modern commentators prefer "altar of incense." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/9-4.htm
  - Constable admits the verse seems to contradict the Old Testament. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-4.html
  - Coffman points out that the text says the inner room "had" the altar, not that the altar stood "in" it. The altar sat right by the veil and belonged to the inner room. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hebrews-9.html
  - Several commentators link the altar to the inner room through the Day of Atonement ritual. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-4.html
  - Precept Austin says that in function the altar belonged to the Most Holy Place, because its incense drifted in there. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_93-5

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says that when God looked into the ark he saw signs of Israel's sin. Once the sacrificial blood was put on the mercy seat, that blood covered his sight of the sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**vv. 6–7**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik's points:
  - Only the high priest went into the inner room, and only once a year, on the Day of Atonement.
  - He went in to make atonement, not for fellowship with God.
  - The Day of Atonement dealt with sins done in ignorance. Known sins were handled by the regular offerings. Jesus' work covers both kinds.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**vv. 8–9**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the old system had to pass away before God's new way could be shown. The word translated "illustration" (*parabole*) means the tabernacle was a kind of parable of the New Covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
- Got Questions says the tabernacle rules show these things never solved sin "once and for all" but pointed ahead to someone who would. https://www.gotquestions.org/appointed-unto-men-once-to-die.html

**v. 11**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Christ serves in a better sanctuary, God's own throne room. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**v. 12**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik's points:
  - The animal was killed outside the veil, but its blood was carried into the inner room. In the same way, Jesus died on earth, but the payment had to be accepted in heaven.
  - The old high priest came back out and the veil stayed shut. Jesus tore the veil and stays inside.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
- **Catholic reading:** Catholic writers lean on this verse. They argue that Christ presents his one offering to the Father in heaven "in a different mode or manner," just as it is made present at Mass. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/the-re-presentation-of-the-mass

**v. 13**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the heifer's ashes were mixed into water used for ceremonial cleansing (Numbers 19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
- **Protestant vs. Catholic:** Guzik also says that because this shadow has been fulfilled, Catholic holy water has no value. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**v. 14**
- **Traditional reading:** Animal blood cleaned the body in a ritual sense. Christ's blood cleans the conscience. Christ also offered himself willingly, while the animals had no will in the matter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/9-14.htm
- **Debate: what is "the eternal Spirit"?** This split runs between teachers, not denominations.
  - **The Holy Spirit:** Piper (Baptist) sees the whole Trinity here: the Son offers, through the Spirit, to the Father. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/purified-to-serve-the-living-god
  - Matthew Henry and Barnes also read it as the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-14.html
  - **Christ's own divine spirit:** Coffman says it is not the Holy Spirit "as usually understood" but Christ's own eternal divine Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-14.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes it as Christ's divine nature, which gives the offering infinite worth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/9-14.htm
  - Wuest takes the same view. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_913-14
  - **Leaving it open:** Ellicott translates "an eternal spirit" and says the usual arguments are not strong enough to justify the standard reading. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/9-14.htm
  - **Calvin (Reformed):** Christ's death should be judged by the Spirit's power, not by the outward act. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-14.html
- **"Dead works":** Guzik says this probably means sin in general ("works that bring death"). It also covers going back to Old Covenant sacrifices. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**v. 15**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says that every sacrifice offered in faith under Moses was like an IOU that was paid in full at the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/

**vv. 16–17**
- **Debate: is the Greek word *diathēkē* a "will" or a "covenant"?**
  - **"Will":** MacArthur explains it as a will: as long as the person who made it is alive, nobody can collect. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1621/the-new-covenant-part-3
  - Ligonier says the writer probably chose the image because the same Greek word means both. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mediator-of-a-new-covenant
  - Guzik (quoting Thomas) thinks the word switches: covenant in v. 15, will in vv. 16–17, covenant again in v. 18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
  - **"Covenant":** Jared Compton (Desiring God) points out the word means "covenant" fifteen other times in Hebrews. He argues the people making the covenant here are sinners, who die through a sacrificial substitute. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/where-theres-not-a-will
  - Vine says calling Christ a "testator" breaks the argument of v. 18. https://www.blueletterbible.org/search/dictionary/viewtopic.cfm?topic=VT0002948
  - Barnes says the person who made it would be "the victim set apart to be slain" to ratify the covenant. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/hebrews/9-16.html

**vv. 18–22**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says nearly every part of the Mosaic system involved blood. People today think sin is forgiven by time, good works or a decent life, but there is no forgiveness without shed blood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
- **Catholic use of v. 22:** One Catholic apologist argues that if the Mass really killed Christ again, it would have to be a bloody sacrifice, because of this verse. Since it is not bloody, it is not a new killing. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/is-the-mass-a-true-sacrifice

**vv. 25–26**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Barnes says that if Christ's blood worked no better than the old offerings, he would have had to die again and again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-26.html
  - Spurgeon says Christ really did put away sin, not just appear to. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-26.html
  - Constable takes "the end of the ages" as the end of the Old Covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-26.html
- **Protestant vs. Catholic (the Mass):**
  - Calvin says those who try to renew Christ's sacrifice insult him, as if his death had not finished everything. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-26.html
  - Guzik calls this passage a direct rebuke of the Mass. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-9/
  - **Catholic answer:** Catholic apologists answer that the Mass does not repeat the cross. It is a "relative sacrifice" that applies the benefits of Christ's one death, which was offered once. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/once-for-all
  - They also say Christ does not die again in the Mass; his death becomes present there. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/is-the-mass-a-true-sacrifice

**v. 27**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Barnes says that because a person dies only once, whatever needs to be done about death must be done before dying. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/hebrews/9-27.html
  - Bible.org says the verse rules out a second chance to accept Christ after death. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-27-judgment-or-salvation-hebrews-923-28
- **Debate: when does judgment happen?**
  - Gill holds to a particular judgment straight after death, and then a universal judgment after the resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/hebrews/9-27.html
  - Barnes is similar. He suggests an informal judgment at death and a final one later. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/hebrews/9-27.html
  - An unnamed older commentary quoted on Bible Hub says Scripture has no word about a particular judgment right after death. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown ties "the judgment" to Christ's appearing in v. 28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/9-27.htm
- **Reincarnation:**
  - Clarke says the verse rules out souls passing from body to body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-27.html
  - The Light of Israel commentary says it rules out reincarnation and karma. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/9-27.html

**v. 28**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The pattern is: people die once and then face judgment, so Christ died once and will come back. Commentators point to the twist that he returns to bring salvation, not judgment, to those waiting for him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_927-28
  - Precept Austin ties "bear the sins of many" to the suffering servant in Isaiah 53. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_927-28
  - Archbishop Tillotson says that at his first coming Christ stood in the place of sinners, but at his second he comes as Judge, not as a sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/9-27.htm
